reasons: In Germany the limit warning is already a feature of invoicing apps: Accountable advertises an alert when users near the 25,000 EUR limit, and kostenlose-erechnung.de sells live limit tracking. Anyone who already invoices in an app sees their turnover there, so a separate meter is a feature, not a product.
Only people close to a limit need it. Most sole traders are far below or far above it, so the paying group in each country is a thin slice.

Six unrelated rule sets (Quebec, Germany, Italy, Netherlands, India, Japan) in five languages means six products to keep legally accurate every year. The Japan evidence rests on private explainers, not the tax office.
The India part is weak: the UPI notice wave of July 2025 was a one-off enforcement event, and small vegetable sellers who got notices are unlikely to pay a monthly app fee.
The best evidence is Quebec, where a CAD 3.99 a month calculator has about 2.8 thousand ratings, so a French-language Quebec app is the most defensible place to start.
verdicts.what_would_change_my_mind: Evidence that many Quebec or German sole traders invoice outside apps (Word, PDF) and would pay for a limit alert on its own, for example paid sign-ups from a single-country landing page.

incumbents: Meezan Bank app linked with Payoneer (Pakistan; generates e-PRC tax documents for Payoneer receipts)

reasons: In Pakistan banks are already building this for free: Payoneer and Meezan Bank are linked so the bank app generates tax documents (e-PRC) for each receipt, and the 0.25% or 1% tax is withheld at source by the bank, so filing is already simple.
In Nigeria the dollar-receiving apps (Cleva, Raenest, Grey) already hold each payout with date and amount and are writing tax guides; adding a free yearly tax statement is an easy move for them.
Guides openly say a simple spreadsheet works, and the need peaks once a year at filing time (31 March in Nigeria, 30 September in Pakistan), so many users will cancel between filings.

Sources disagree on core rules in all three countries (Section 65F credit in Pakistan, whether export income counts toward the monotributo cap, which CBN rate to use), so the app carries liability for wrong figures, and three countries means three rulebooks.
Plus side: these users earn in dollars and often hold dollar cards, so paying $2-3 a month is practical.
verdicts.what_would_change_my_mind: Evidence that Nigerian or Pakistani freelancers already pay accountants for this, or that Cleva, Raenest and Payoneer partner banks will not add tax statements.

reasons: Free state tools already exist in two of the five countries: Turkey's GIB portal issues e-SMM receipts for free, and Poland has the free KSeF taxpayer app plus free e-Mikrofirma, so the paid value there is only alerts and convenience.

UAE e-invoicing must go through accredited service providers (ASPs). Vendor estimates put an ASP subscription at about AED 2,000-10,000 a year for small firms. A solo founder cannot easily become an ASP, and a partner's cost per user could exceed a $2-3 price. Saudi Wave 25 covers firms above SAR 187,500 turnover (about USD 50,000). These are not micro-sellers; they already pay SAR 60-140 a month, and the free FatooraZ app exists for very small ones.

Five countries means five certified integrations (ZATCA onboarding, UAE Peppol via an ASP, Egypt ETA, a Turkish integrator, KSeF), each with its own certification and security demands. That is a heavy build for a $2-3 product.
The need itself is well evidenced (deadlines, fines, competitor prices), especially in the UAE; the risk is cost and certification, not demand.
verdicts.what_would_change_my_mind: A UAE ASP or Saudi integrator quote for white-label API access at under about $0.50 per user a month, and confirmation that there is no free-100-invoices rule in the UAE.

reasons: In Mexico, individuals with platform income up to 300,000 pesos a year can choose to treat the platform withholding as final (pago definitivo): no monthly provisional filings and often no annual return. For most part-time sellers there is nothing to credit and no risk of paying twice, which removes the core pitch.

Sellers above that cap, and Philippine sellers above PHP 500,000, are serious businesses that usually use an accountant or full accounting software. They are a smaller group and expect more than a $2 app.
For EU DAC7, private sellers of used goods usually owe no tax; the need is reassurance once a year in January, which is seasonal and weak for a monthly plan.
The marketplaces (Mercado Libre, Shopee, Lazada) hold all the data and already issue certificates; they can add a free tax summary to the seller centre at any time.
Four regions with different regimes, and Indonesia's PMK 37/2025 threshold and start date are still unclear in the sources.
verdicts.what_would_change_my_mind: Evidence that a large share of Mexican or Philippine platform sellers are above the final-withholding caps and do their own filings without an accountant.
